analysis.one_liner: Requires carmakers to sell safety features separately instead of bundling them into pricier trim packages.
analysis.headline: A bill requiring automakers to offer crash-avoidance safety features on their own, not bundled into luxury trims, cleared a House subcommittee by voice vote but has never reached a full committee vote or the House floor.
analysis.plain_summary: Some carmakers sell features that help avoid crashes — automatic emergency braking, lane-keeping alerts, drowsy-driver warnings, automatic crash notification — only in expensive trim levels or option packages. This bill would force them to sell those features separately or make them standard, and to show buyers the price of each safety feature on its own. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the rule, with the change kicking in 180 days after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Car buyers, especially people shopping at lower price points who are currently pushed toward costlier trims to get features that alert them to crashes, keep them in their lane, watch for fatigue or impairment, improve headlights and visibility, or call emergency services after a wreck. State attorneys general would gain a new tool to sue on residents' behalf, with fees recoverable if they win.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car buyers priced out of safety trims

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits selling or leasing an optional safety feature unless it is offered separately from non-safety features or made standard equipment, and requires a clear, separate disclosure of its price [S2].

It covers features that control vehicle motion, warn of collision risk or lane drift, flag distracted, fatigued, or impaired driving, improve road illumination and visibility, alert emergency services after a crash, or other safety functions the FTC and the Transportation Department add later [S2].

Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the Federal Trade Commission Act, enforced by the FTC, and state attorneys general can sue to stop the practice, impose civil penalties, and win restitution or damages for residents [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, which would lose the ability to charge a premium for safety by bundling it into higher trims, and to some extent buyers if manufacturers raise base prices to offset lost trim revenue. The FTC takes on enforcement work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Automakers, and possibly buyers via base prices

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers and dealers would face new pricing, labeling, and compliance costs within 180 days of enactment, and some of those costs could be passed to buyers through higher base prices — the bill mandates separate sale but does not cap prices [S2].

The requirement applies only to a vehicle's first purchaser and only to the specific safety functions defined in the bill or later added by the FTC, leaving room for features that do not fit the definitions to remain bundled [S2].
It is a disclosure-and-separation rule rather than a mandate that any car include the safety features; a buyer with no extra budget still cannot afford the feature, only see its price clearly [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — safety technology that prevents crashes becoming available to buyers at every price point, with honest pricing — is real and addressed to a genuine practice of gating safety behind luxury packages. The main costs are compliance burden and possible base-price increases, which could partially offset the gain for budget buyers. On balance a modest, well-targeted consumer protection, though it relies on FTC follow-through and does not require any car to actually include the features.

outcome.mechanism: It is still alive but barely moving: a House subcommittee approved it by voice vote on February 10, 2026, and the full Energy and Commerce Committee has not taken it up since, with no House vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on February 4, 2026, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade [S1][S4].
The subcommittee held a consideration and markup session on February 10, 2026, and forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote [S4].
As of the latest record, no further committee action has occurred, no cosponsors have joined, and the House has not voted [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers keep the status quo: safety features can stay bundled into expensive trim packages while the bill waits in committee. Car buyers are no worse off than before, but gain nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers keep the trim-bundling status quo

for.name: Frank Pallone
for.role: U.S. Representative (NJ) and sponsor; Ranking Member, House Energy and Commerce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and saw it through subcommittee referral; as the committee's top Democrat he advanced it through the subcommittee of jurisdiction.

against.name: Brett Guthrie
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a full committee markup of the bill since the subcommittee forwarded it by voice vote on February 10, 2026, leaving it without a committee vote or a path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Only one Democrat has sponsored the bill, no Republican has cosponsored it, and no vote has been recorded, so the partisan shape is not yet visible [S3].

industries.note: The bill takes away their ability to charge a premium for crash-avoidance features by bundling them into higher trims or option packages, and requires separate price disclosure. For buyers, the industry's gain in the current bundling model is the public's cost — safety held behind a paywall — so its interest in keeping that model runs against consumers.

Dealers sell the trim packages, so separate sale and disclosure of safety-feature pricing constrains how they present and price optional equipment. The bill applies to whoever offers the feature for sale to a first purchaser, which includes dealers.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, a single Democratic sponsor, and no full-committee action more than a week after subcommittee approval, the bill is very likely to sit in committee for the rest of this Congress unless it attracts broader support or is folded into a larger vehicle-safety or consumer package.
